title: Victor sessions, Charles Smith and Morton's dispute over copyrights
summary: How the Victor New Orleans Jazzmen sides came about, Morton's view of the trumpeter De Paris, and the copyright and leadership argument.

bands.name: Jelly Roll Morton's New Orleans Jazzmen

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well, how did you ever get general records interested? Was that Charles Smith that got them started?

Charles Smith is to be credited with that, yes. You see, he wrote that book and they gave quite a boost there. And I think Charles Smith and maybe some other boys up there interested Victor and those Victor sides that he made with his New Orleans Jazzmen.
That's when he got Bichet with him and Nicholas and De Paris.

But Jellie didn't like De Paris as a trumpet player. He liked him as a player, but he was an obstinate man, I think. He didn't like to be told how to play or why I think. That's the best I can gather from it. Jellie never mentioned his name, but in talking about it later, he says the trumpet player did his best to spoil things or something like that. He said he didn't want to follow instructions, I don't know why.
Well, I guess they figured George Jellie, being the way he was, he came up there, you know. He knew more buzz than any of them and they didn't.

They knew something about it. There was a little episode also about that, you know. As soon as they, they made two sides, I don't know, a couple of sides first. And Jellie was the leader and he arranged the studio arrangements for them, as much as they needed. Jazzmen, that he knew like the bunch that was there, Claude Jones and Baixier and the rest, didn't need much arrangement for them, but Jellie arranged for them. And he, they came to him and said, all right Jellie, now sign us the copyrights and we'll go ahead and put these out. He says, copyrights are owned in Washington. Washington, who buys? They're a Temple Music Publishing Company in Washington, no one saw it. He says, they do? You don't own them? He says, no. He says, well, he says, next, they told him that, he says, the next, the next one's re-recorded, so-and-so will be the leader. See, I don't know who he mentioned. And Jellie says, I know what that meant. It meant that I'd do the arranging and he'd get the credit and pay for it. Yeah. Because the other fellow couldn't arrange whoever he was. Oh, I see.
He's going to make somebody else a leader.
Yeah, make somebody else a leader. Did that happen? I doubt if it happened.
I don't know. I don't think it happened. No, I don't think so. Because Jellie, the second session was, well, it was two weeks later, actually. Yeah. According to this.
I don't think it happened, but they-
Of course, Baixier wasn't on that session.
No, he was only on the first. Yeah, so. They have great records, those four records.
